speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. KENNEDY (Peace River) moved:
maintopic: EDMONTON, DUNVEGAN AND BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY COMPANY MOTION THAT BILL BE GIVEN PRECEDENCE
speechtext:
That all unopposed private bills placed on the order paper for consideration from 8 to 9 p.m. on Tuesday, the 1st of May, 1928, be then given precedence over other bills.
My purpose in moving this motion, Mr. Speaker, is to enable the house to pass-without prejudice to other private bills-bill No. 57, which stands as order No. 56 under private bills. It is "an act respecting the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia Railway Company." I am asking the house to table this course because of a telegram I have received from the Department of Railways and Telephones in Alberta, reading as follows:
Please advise when sanction of E D and B C legislation authorising extensions of main line and Grande Prairie branch may be expected. Very essential that construction of Grande Prairie branch extension be started at once in order that grading be completed before winter owing to advanced state of settlement in

Edmonton, Dunvegan Railway
locality to be served by proposed railway extension. In public interest that railway facilities be provided early as possible. Wire reply.
(Signed) Jno Callaghan.
I may say that an early start on this railway will make a difference of a season and accommodate settlers who are now living from thirty to seventy miles from railway facilities and raising from a million to a million and a quarter bushels of grain. Consequently the Alberta government, having made an appropriation for this railway extension, are anxious to start work as quickly as possible.
The bill finds itself in its present position through a collision with the rules, which apparently none of us thought of when we asked on April 17 that it stand. When the bill was in committee a mistake was discovered in the wording of a certain amendment. Let me illustrate my point by quoting from Hansard of that date:
Mr. Dunning: Ferhaps the hon. member for Peace River would consent to leave the bill in committee in order that he may determine what amendment should be made.
Mr. Cahill: If the figures are not right there must have been an error on my part in putting them down. In that case I hardly think it necessary to give notice of an amendment.
Mr. Kennedy: I am quite certain that in subsection (a) the words should be seventy-eight or seventy-nine. And in subsection (b) seventy-seven or seventy-eight.
Mr. Dunning: If my hon. friend is prepared to move an amendment now, in view of the fact that apparently there is a clerical error in the record we may dispense with the usual notice. In any event the mistake must be corrected by some formal action on the part of this committee. I suggest to my hon. friend that he leave the bill in committee in order to enable him to confirm his impression, or he may move the necessary substitution now.
Therefore I would ask the house to agree to this motion.

reason why one private bill should be given preference over any other. The government is anxious that all of these bills should be reached, and if hon. gentlemen will co-operate with us we will do our utmost to expedite the final disposition of all the private bills.
I do not think we can single out one particular bill and at the same time disregard all the others.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this bill would have gone through the house the other night except for a clerical error-purely unintentional-on the part of the chairman of the railway committee. maintopic: EDMONTON, DUNVEGAN AND BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY COMPANY MOTION THAT BILL BE GIVEN PRECEDENCE

maintopic: EDMONTON, DUNVEGAN AND BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY COMPANY MOTION THAT BILL BE GIVEN PRECEDENCE

Edmonton, Dunvegan Railway

maintopic: EDMONTON, DUNVEGAN AND BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY COMPANY MOTION THAT BILL BE GIVEN PRECEDENCE
speechtext: Of that particular bill.

maintopic: EDMONTON, DUNVEGAN AND BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY COMPANY MOTION THAT BILL BE GIVEN PRECEDENCE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: EDMONTON, DUNVEGAN AND BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY COMPANY MOTION THAT BILL BE GIVEN PRECEDENCE
speechtext: I was in the house at the time, but I did not recognize at the moment the fact that it was with reference to that particular discussion that this motion was being put. We have had to wait two days in succession-a Friday and a Tuesday-for private bills to come up. They have been held up. These private bills have had no oportunity of being considered by the house.

I remember perfectly well the incident that occurred the other evening, and the hon. member who said "Stand" was the hon. gentleman himself. Why therefore should we be deprived of our rights at the present time? I may point out that there is an important bill of mine first on the order paper for consideration of the house to-morrow evening at eight o'clock. Why should I give way, notwithstanding the rules of the house, when my bill stands first for consideration? I do not see any reason and I protest.

maintopic: EDMONTON, DUNVEGAN AND BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY COMPANY MOTION THAT BILL BE GIVEN PRECEDENCE

There are on the order paper other bills which, to a number of us, are just as important as the measure in which the hon. member who is moving this motion is interested. I do not see why there should be a departure from the ordinary rules and orders in dealing with these bills as a class by singling out one particular bill in order to accommodate some hon. member. I suggest that the proper, procedure would be to segregate the divorce bills from the other bills and, if you are going to give special attention to any one, then consider those measures, other than divorce bills in their order.

I do not think the hon. member for Rimouski, and the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat, are quite correct in their premises in this matter. There is no special privilege asked for this bill. What really happened was this: there was an error in the work of the King's Printer in regard to a numeral. When the bill came before the house the minister in charge did not know whether it was correct or whether the statement of those in this corner was right. It was found that the position taken by us in this corner was the correct one. Through no fault of ours but by reason of an error on the part of the King's Printer, or whoever prints these bills, and possibly at least on the part of the chairman of the railway committee, the bill has been unfairly put at the foot of the list. Had the bill been properly printed it would have gone through the house without question the other night. It is not unfair therefore to suggest that in view of most peculiar and unusual circumstances such as these the public interest could be better served if the house were considerate, in this particular instance at any rate. I agree absolutely with the hon. member for Rimouski on principle as regards the consideration of these bills. I do not think that any bill should be given precedence over others, and for that reason I voted the other night against

Edmonton, Dunvegan Railway

Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals):	If I may be permitted to clarify the situation with respect to this bill, it was a private bill with which the government had nothing to do. It went to the railway committee in the usual way and there, following a discussion,, was amended in ink by the chairman in connection with certain numerals. maintopic: EDMONTON, DUNVEGAN AND BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY COMPANY MOTION THAT BILL BE GIVEN PRECEDENCE

The chairman of the railway committee, who is not present to-day, stated on that occasion that if there was an error doubtless it could be attributed to him. To avoid the necessity for formal notice, he was willing to take the responsibility of having made a clerical error himself, and under those circumstances I suggested that if the hon. member for Peace River was sure enough of the correct numerals, we might decide to let the bill go through without the customary notice of motion for an amendment to a private bill. In the interests of accuracy, my hon. friend from Peace River being Scotch, and desiring to be absolutely sure, he decided, and properly, to let the bill stand. As to its coming up again first to-morrow night, I of course have no objection. If the same attitude is taken towards this bill as is taken towards other private bills by hon. members in the opposite corner of the house and by the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church), those who object can easily talk for the full hour to-morrow night. Immigration Act
Mr. Speaker, many of the members of the house have made engagements for this first Wednesday evening.

The house resumed from April 27 consideration in committee of Bill No. 187, to amend the Immigration Act-Mr. Forke-Mr. March in the chair.	.
On section 1-Persons deemed to belong to prohibited classes.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few remarks with.regard to this bill, notwithstanding the fact that it has been before the house on numerous occasions. I object to section 41 of the Immigration Act as it now stands and I do so on two grounds: first, it discriminates, in my opinion very unfairly, against British subjects who were born outside of Canada; in the second place, the legislation is unnecessary in view of the other provisions of the Immigration Aijt and in view of the provisions of the criminal code and the common law with regard to sedition.
The discrimination, I think, is admitted. The section as it stands places British subjects who were born outside of Canada in an inferior position to aliens who have become naturalized as British subjects in Canada Section 3 of the Immigration Act specifies the classes of persons who are to be regarded as undesirable or prohibited classes. Section 41, which we are now discussing, refers to several classes of offences and provides that the persons who commit those offences shall be deemed to come within the undesirable classes. Section 42 provides for the method of deportation of those who are, under the provisions of the Act, deemed to be undesirable. Section 41 of the act has an important proviso at the end thereof, which I propose to read:
Provided, that this section shall not apply to any person who is a British subject, either by reason of birth in Canada, or by reason of naturalization in Canada.
Thus it happens that a British subject who comes to Canada is not exempted from the provisions of this act because he cannot be naturalized in Canada. He is a British subject by virtue of his having become such somewhere outside of Canada. So that the section as it reads does not apply to persons who are born in Canada or to aliens who have become naturalized as British subjects in Canada, but it does extend to British subjects who come to Canada from some other part of the empire. It would apply, for example, to anyone who was born in
England or Scotland or any other of the British dominions. British subjects born outside of Canada can never become exempt from the provisions of this section; so that it follows that a naturalized alien may commit any of the offences described in section 41, and he is not deemed to be an undesirable and he cannot be deported; but persons who happen to have been born in England or Scotland who do commit any of the offences described in section 41 are deemed to be undesirable and are subject to deportation. An alien may become naturalized, if I remember the provisions of the Naturalization Act correctly, after five years residence in Canada. He then under the provisions of the Immigration Act is exempt from deportation; but a British subject born outside of Canada cannot never get complete exemption from deportation, no matter how long he resides in Canada. So that you have this situation; even if a naturalized alien commits one of the offences referred to in section 41 and is convicted of that offence after full trial by a jury, he cannot be deported; but a British subject born outside of Canada may commit one of the less important offences referred to in section 41 and he can be deported without any trial, on the mere say-so of a single officer of the department. That is a discrimination which ought not to exist in any British statute. The statute as it stands discriminates in this manner against a British subject born outside of	Canada, and	I	think	the legaleffect of the section is beyond dispute. I will go further and say that the change in the law was deliberately made to make this discrimination possible;	it	was	intendedspecifically	for British subjects born outside
of Canada and for no one else.
Why?

I will ask the committee
to follow irfe carefully with regard to the history of	the passage	of	this	legislation
through the house and in the comparison which I make between the section as it now stands and the state of the law as it existed prior to the enactment of this section. In the discussion of last year a comparison was made between the state of the law as it is now under the provisions of this section and as it was in 1910 when the Immigration Act was first passed. I do not think that is the comparison which ought to be made. I think the comparison ought to be made between the section as it now stands and the section that was passed in the same session of parliament, because in the session of 1919 two bills were brought in to amend the Immigration Act.
Immigration Act

One of them, which appears in the statutes of 1919 as chapter 25, comprised twenty-six sections including an amendment to section 41. In the same session another bill was introduced which appeai-s as chapter 26 of the statutes of 1919 and it includes only one section, the one which we are now discussing.
The first bill to amend the Immigration Act was comprehensive in its nature and it subjected the Immigration Act to a careful and thorough revision. It was introduced into the house and received first reading on the 7th April, 1919. It received second reading and went into committee on the 29th April. It received third reading on the 12th May. In the senate it received first reading on the 15th May, second reading on the 16th May and third reading on the 4th June. The senate reported the bill with an amendment which I will not discuss but which does not deal with the points which we have under consideration. The senate amendment was concurred in on the 5th June and on the 6th June the bill received royal assent. The section of which we now complain was not included in that bill. The present section 41 was introduced into the House of Commons on the 6th June fifteen minutes before the house was summoned to appear before the senate to hear the royal assent being given to the bills which had passed both houses of parliament prior to that time. It was introduced, received first and second readings, passed through the committee stage and received third reading, all in fifteen minutes.
When?
On the 6th June.
What year?
Just as a matter of information, will the hon. member explain what he means by "railroaded through the House of Commons?"

I think the term has a fairly well-known meaning. What was the reason for this unseemly haste in bringing this bill into legislative effect, that is' within half an hour of its first introduction into the house? I think I am conservative in making that estimate of time. It was law half an hour after it was first introduced into the House of Commons. In Hansard, page 3211, of the 1919 debates, Hon. J. A. Calder, Minister of Immigration, in introducing the bill said:
In the bill which was before this house amending the Immigration Act certain persons who advocated the overthrow of government, the destruction of property, and so on, by violence, were within the prohibited classes. The matter has been inquired into further and the law officers of the crown have advised that the section as it stands does not really cover all that was intended.
What was intended? I have made the Statement that the intention of the amendment was to discriminate against British subjects born outside of Canada, and to enable their deportation without a trial. That is what was intended.
What reasons were given in the House of Commons for the enactment of this measure? The leader of the opposition, Mr. D. D. McKenzie, asked in the course of the debate, "How does the new clause differ from the old?" The hon. member for Gaspe, Mr. APRIL 30, 1928
Immigration Act
Lemieux, later in the course of the debate asked, "Would the minister point out where it differs as he goes along?" To which, Mr. Calder replied, "It is not the easiest thing in the world to do." Then Mr. Calder indicated certain respects in which the bill differed from the bill previously introduced and concurred in by both houses' of parliament dealing with section 41, and he indicated every difference except the difference that is the real difference, the difference of which we are complaining. In order to make that point perfectly clear, it is necessary for me to refer to the state of the law as it existed prior to the passing of this act of which we are complaining. Section 41 as passed previously in the same session commences in this manner:
Whenever any person, other than a Canadian citizen advocates in Canada the overthrow by force-
I shall not read the balance. The importance of what I am saying apears from the words which I have just quoted, namely: "Whenever any person other than a Canadian citizen" commits the following offences he shall be considered an undesirable. That is, anybody who was a Canadian citizen, no matter how he got his Canadian citizenship, was exempted from deportation under the provisions of the act as it stood prior to the enactment of this section. But the new section 41 commences in this manner: "Every person who commits" the following offences is an undesirable, and it concludes with the proviso:
Provided, that this section shall not apply to any person who is a British subject, either by reason of birth in Canada, or by reason of naturalization in Canada.
So that the effect of removing the opening words of the old section, "whenever any person other than a Canadian citizen," and the tacking on of the proviso of the new section, is to make a discrimination against British subjects who were born outside of Canada.

May I ask whether the
hon. gentleman would be in favour of the substitution of section 41 as it stood before being amended by this act?

I shall deal with that
point a little later. The words "Canadian citizen" as used in the Immigration Act have a special significance. The term is defined in paragraph (f) of section 2 of the Immigration Act, as follows:
"Canadian citizen" means-
1.	a person born in Canada who has not become an alien;
2.	a British subject who has Canadian domicile: or,
3.	a person naturalized under the laws of Canada who has not subsequently become an alien or lost Canadian domicile.
That is, it has a special meaning as it is used in the Immigration Act. The word "domicile" is defined also.

Would the hon. gentleman allow me to repeat my question? In view of his explanation of what constitutes a Canadian citizen, would he be in favour of substituting the original section 41 for the section which is now under discussion?

I have already stated,
and in this I think I have the support of the hon. leader of the opposition, that section 41 is of no value in view of the other provisions of the Immigration Act and of the code. I shall come back to that in a moment.
That is no answer to the question.

I do not propose to be
diverted from my line of discussion. The word "domicile" is also defined in the act, in paragraph (d) of section 2, as follows:
"domicile" means the place in which a person has his home, or in which he resides, or to which he returns as his place of permanent abode, and does not mean the place where he resides for a mere special or temporary purpose;
(i)	Canadian domicile can only be acquired, for the purposes of this act, by a person having his domicile for at least five years in Canada after having been landed therein within the meaning of this act;
So that Canadian domicile has a special meaning under this act and must not be confused with the ordinary meaning attached to the word domicile. Therefore, under the old law, a British subject born outside of Canada who had lived in Canada and acquired Canadian domicile, by virtue of his acquisition of Canadian domicile became a Canadian citizen and was exempted from deportation. Now under the new law he is expressly discriminated against because under section 41 every person who commits any of the offences therein mentioned is classed as an undesirable and is liable to deportation without trial; but there is a proviso that the section does not apply to British subjects who are such by virtue of birth in Canada or by reason of naturalization in Canada. In other words, the British subject born outside of Canada remains constantly liable to deportation, and under another section of the act he can never acquire Canadian domicile in order to exempt himself from deportation under section 41.
I make the statement that in the course of the debate in tho House of Commons when this section was being discussed, all the differences were pointed out to the house except the important ur.d major difference, but the purpose of the amending act was clearly
?498
Immigration Act

indicated in the debate which took place in the senate. I therefore make the statement that legislation of this sort which so unjustly discriminates against one class of British subject is iniquitous legislation and ought not to be tolerated for one moment on the statute books of this parliament.
I think no one will deny that as section 41 now stands there is this discrimination. I would go further and say that section 41 is not needed in view of the other provisions of the Immigration Act and the provisions of the criminal code. Sections 3 and 40 of the Immigration Act sufficiently provide for some of the offences described in section 41. The other offences are, I think, amply provided for by the criminal code. I do not seek to minimize or in any way condone the seriousness of the offences referred to in section 41, but I say advisedly, after careful consideration, that section 41 is not necessary in view of the provisions which we already have in the Immigration Act and in the criminal code. So that the only purpose of maintaining section 41 is to continue the discrimination against British subjects born outside of Canada.
I make that statement with a large measure of support from no less a lawyer than the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). He has spoken twice on this subject in previous sessions. In 1926, when a private member, he agreed with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) that if section 40 of the Immigration Act were retained-and there is no suggestion that it be not-then section 41 was valueless and of no importance. So there may be no question of this, let me quote this most important statement. It will be found at page 4120 of Hansard of June 7, 1926:
Mr. Lapointe: But we must keep the bill in order to repeal section 41. I am quite willing to agree with the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) to allow the bill to read:
"Section 41 of the Immigration Act, chapter 27 of the Statutes of 1910, as enacted by chapter 26 of the statutes of 1919, is repealed."
The rest is certainly covered by section 40.
Mr. Bennett: That is my view.
Earlier in the debate the hon. member for W.est Calgary said:
Then section 41 is of no value at all, or it should be linked up in some way with section 40.
Mr. Cannon: Section 40 covers the case.
Mr. Lapointe: I agree that section 40 would cover the ease, and the only purpose of the bill would be to repeal section 41.
Mr. Bennett: The new section is of no value at all.
Speaking again on this subject last session the language of the hon. member for West

Calgary was somewhat different. At page 2103 of Hansard of April 27, 1927, I find the following:
I do say, sir, that the maintaining of that section upon our statute books was never more necessary than it is to-day.
The same section that was absolutely valueless the year before!

That is a mistake. I
was referring to the section as a whole, not a part of it.

I have no doubt that
my hon. friend will be quite able to look after himself when his turn comes.

Deal with the whole of
it.

I will continue the quotation from the point where I was interrupted:
Having regard for what is going on to-day in China, having regard to the deliberate concerted effort that is being made to destroy the British Empire, openly vaunted by a certain class of people in the world who are teaching sedition in the worst form and endeavouring in every way possible to bring about the destruction of the empire, this statute should remain just where it is in order that if the occasion necessitates we may use it, and use it effectively.
The same statute that in his opinion was valueless the year before. Then at page 2104
he says:
Deportation is not punishment.
Well, I should like to know what could be more drastic punishment than the deportation of a British subject born outside of Canada who has lived here for twenty years, whose roots have been torn up from the soil of Great Britain and planted here. Yet the hon. gentleman says that deportation in such a case is not punishment.
The criminal law is in operation for the punishment of the offender, and for deterring others; it is to punish those who violate our laws. But deportation is to send out of our country undesirable citizens, and when this house votes to repeal a section such as that, indirectly it says that it is satisfied that that class of person is not an undesirable person. To retain the section cannot do harm; it may do good. It cannot interefere with liberty, because it does not deal with British subjects.
In fairness to the hon. member I may say that I think he read the section with which we are now dealing a little too rapidly, for he stated several times that section 41 as it now stands did not apply to British subjects. I also wish to say that he corrected that statement later on in the course of the debate. I quote from Hansard at page 2110 of April 8, 1927:
Mr. Bennett: Rising to a question of privilege, I have to thank my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) for

Immigration Act
having drawn my attention to the fact that I used the words "British subject" erroneously.
I was speaking very rapidly.-
That is liow he spoke on Friday night.

-I was speaking very rapidly and should have employed the expression "Canadian citizen" instead of which I erroneously used the term "British citizen or subject" and did so quite frequently.
Mr. Forke: You used the term "British subject" several times.
Mr. Bennett: I know I did, hut I did so erroneously, and I now desire to make a correction.
Perhaps a certain latitude ought to be allowed to private members of the opposition This year, however, the hon. member for West Calgary occupies an important position as the head of a great party. Perhaps in view of the statements made by him in 1926 that the section was valueless, and in 1927 that it was most important that it should be retained, he will communicate to this house his present views on this subject now that he is the leader of the Conservative party.
In support of my contention that the legislation is not only discriminatory against British subjects born outside of Canada, but is also of no value having regard to the existing law, I repeat that section 3 of the Immigration Act is very wide in its extent. Section 40 is wide in its extent and the provisions of the criminal law with regard to sedition are generously very broad indeed. Section 132 of the criminal code has been frequently referred to in the course of the discussion on this subject:
Seditious words are words expressive of a seditious intention.
(2)	A seditious libel is a libel expressive of a seditious intention,
(3)	A seditious conspiracy is an agreement between two or more persons to carry into execution a seditious intention.
Then 134 provides for the punishment of sedition. But the expression "seditious intention" is nowhere defined in the criminal code, and therefore we have to go back to the English common law, which is the law of this country except in so far as it has been changed by statute. As I say, the definition of seditious intention appears nowhere in the criminal code. When it was intended in England to draft a code of English criminal law section 102 was drawn up, but it never became law. It did, however, contain a clause defining seditious intention. I cite now Crank-shaw's Criminal Code at page 142:

or either house of parliament, or the administration of justice; or to excite Her Majesty's subjects to attempt to procure, otherwise than by law-ful means, the alteration of any matter-

I therefore make the statement in conclusion that this section as it stands now is unjust in that it discriminates unfairly against British subjects born outside Canada. It is also unnecessary in view of the legislation already existing. I therefore appeal to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) to assist in the repeal of this iniquitous law. It is a monstrosity that bears the obvious signs of its hysterical birth. There ought not to be in this country any legislation that effects or makes possible discrimination of this sort. Canadian citizenship ought to mean the same for all Canadian citizens. Canadian citizenship is something that ought to be valued, and we ought to place all persons who are British subjects on the same footing, whether they are British subjects born in Canada or British subjects born outside Canada, whether they are British subjects by virtue of birth or by naturalization. When we hand ian alien a certificate of naturalization we say to him, "You have served five years of probation in this country and we deem you a fit person to enjoy the rights and privileges of British citizenship now conferred upon you". Let us place all British subjects in this country upon an equality. We cannot do so without repealing this section. I therefore again appeal to the leader of the opposition to assist the house in bringing about that repeal. He now occupies an important position and irresponsible utterances do not come well from him.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the committee rose at six o'clock we were considering Bill 187, to amend the Immigration Act. The discussion is on section 1, persons deemed to belong to prohibited classes.

Mr. Chairman, as the
committee rose we were discussing a question of order raised by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). Perhaps it will satisfy all the purposes I had in mind if I say there was no bargain other than that to which I referred on the records of the House of Commons. The hon. member quite appreciates that I was not casting any reflection upon him in the matter.
There is just one other point I desire to deal with-that raised by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), when he intimated that the making of a report did not signify that action would necessarily be taken. Section 42 of the Immigration Act deals with that situation:
Upon receiving a complaint from any officer, or from any clerk or secretary or other official of a municipality, whether directly or through the superintendent of Immigration, against any person alleged to belong to any prohibited or undesirable class, the minister may order such person to be taken into custody and detained at an immigrant station for examination and an
investigation of the facts alleged in the said complaint to be made by a board of inquiry or by an officer acting as such. Such board of inquiry or officer shall have the same powers and privileges, and shall follow the same procedure, as if the person against whom complaint is made were being examined before landing as provided in section 33, of this act; and similarly the person against whom complaint is made shall have the same rights and privileges as he would have if seeking to land in Canada.
2.	If upon investigation of the facts such board of inquiry or examining officer is satisfied that such person belongs to any of the prohibited or undesirable classes mentioned in sections 40 and 41 of this act, such person shall be deported forthwith, as provided for in section 33 of this act, subject, however, to such right of appeal as he may have to the minister.
3.	The governor in council may, at any time, order any such person found by a board of inquiry or examining officer to belong to any of the undesirable classes referred to in section 41 of this act to leave Canada within a specified period. Such order may be in the form D in the schedule to this act, and shall be in force as soon as it is served upon such person, or is left for him by any officer at the last known place of abode or address of such person.
There are other subsections, but I need not quote them now.
That applies to aliens.

No, to everybody. It
follows section 41 as it now reads. That is the point I am making. It refers in terms to all persons subject to deportation. I mention that in order that there may be no misapprehension as to the scope and authority of the section to which I refer.
There is one other fact which I think has been overlooked and which I venture to bring to the attention of my hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Thorson). Section 41, which is now sought to be repealed, contains this proviso:
Provided that this section shall not apply to any person who is a British subject, either by reason of birth in Canada, or by reason of naturalisation in Canada.
That is the proviso to which so much objection is taken. May I point out to him and other hon. members that that applies to immigrants from Australia or New Zealand or Newfoundland or India or South Africa, and to endeavour to limit the scope and operation of the section to those who come from the British Isles is manifestly wrong.

I did not so limit the
scope of the section.

It was just the inference
drawn by the minister speaking in relation to the matter, when my friend from Vancouver Centre was dealing with that phase of it. This section in terms applies to the seditionist whether he be from 'India, Australia, South Africa, New Zealand-in fact to any person
Immigration Act

who comes within the description of "British subject" regardless of what part of the empire he may come from. I desire to make that clear. Let me summarize this and I have concluded for the moment. First, this country claims a right to deport, for causes that may be determined by parliament, any immigrant who may come within its borders. An immigrant may come from one of two places-outside of or within the British Empire. For the purposes of this act the person who comes from without the British Empire is treated as being in exactly the same position as the person who comes from within; they stand upon parity.
But not deportable.

Yes, exactly. The immigrant who comes from without the British Empire and the immigrant who comes from within stand upon a parity. I know what my hon. friend is going to say, but perhaps he will wait until he hears my next sentence. There is no power to deport a Canadian. Therefore, with respect to naturalized aliens this section has no application; but inasmuch as a British subject, whether he come from England, or India or Australia or New Zealand, is at the end of five years undeportable by reason of' 'the limitation imposed (by the statute, for I apprehend that the terms of the section are not sufficient to afford the minister power after five years-

the act?

The section that deals
with the limitation of five years. It used to be three, if my memory serves me right.

Oh yes, if he wrere convicted under the criminal code.

Why should he be? He is not guilty until found so.

Since the Immigration
Act was first passed, we have said: We are going to deport undesirables after investigation by a board of inquiry. Every other nation does the same.

Of the country.

friend from Winnipeg South Centre read it to-day. That was a class of immigrants who had to be dealt with in some way, and this country asserted its sovereign power. under this act to be deprived of all rights to trial.

speechtext:

Immigration Act

That begs the question.
The issue, which is a simple one, is this: The parliament of Canada in 1919, for reasons which it considered sound, and with the approval of the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and of the Liberal party, unanimously enacted this statute. The statute i3 now sought to be repealed. Has anyone been injured under it? Has any wrong been done? Is it desirable to remove from the statute book a provision which parliament in 1919 deemed desirable? Let us get down to that question. My hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre suggested that in 1926 I dealt with the question in one way, and in 1927 in another. I turned up the record and this is the position I took: in both cases I declared that it was not desirable to repeal the statute. Although it might work a hardship there had been no cases under it, so far as I could see; and it was meant only for that class of immigrants who openly and notoriously preached sedition in this country. I went further. The statute of 1926 had substituted another section, and the discussion between the Minister of Justice and myself was a discussion as to what the meaning was if it should be passed in the form in which it was proposed. I held that it meant nothing if the contention he put forward was correct. But upon the question as to the desirability of repealing the statute, hon. members will find that my observations were practically the same in both cases, except for one circumstance. I happened to be on the train a few days previously, in one case, and I referred to certain articles that had appeared in the newspapers with reference to the preaching of sedition in one of our towns-* naming the place-from which seditious literature was being disseminated. That fact I alluded to. But with respect to the question itself, my remarks were the same on both occasions. The committee will recall, however, that in 1926 an endeavour was made to substitute a new section for that which was being repealed; whereas in the present instance it is not proposed to make any substitution at all.
Now let me conclude; I was about to summarize my observations when the minister asked me a question. It is conceded to be the right of all free people to determine who shall come within their boundaries.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Hear, hear.
Hear, hear.

The Canadian people, in parliament assembled, have determined that certain classes may be deported without trial.

That has been so ever since the law was passed, and in 1910 Sir Wilfrid Laurier revised the whole Immigration Act, once more recognizing that principle. In 1919 parliament extended the law in its application to the number of persons who should come under it, including those who preached and taught sedition. That was the extension of the provision embracing those who could be deported without trial. That was all.
It was much more than that.

It merely extended the
class.
It was much wider than my hon. friend suggests.

It extended the class to
all persons who were not Canadians; it included the alien immigrant who had not become naturalized and who therefore had to go, if he came within the terms of the law. And the British subject, whether he came from Hong Kong, from New Zealand or from Great Britain, was also subject to deportation if he come within the terms of the statute. That is all; nothing more and nothing less.

That is the thing we object
to.

That is precisely what the statute says; provided that it shall not apply to two classes, the British subject who was born in this country and who was given a status at once, and the naturalized Canadian. These could not be deported, and that for the reasons given this afternoon by the minister.

You claim that people
bom in Great Britain never become Canadians.

Not at all. The minister has overlooked the fact that this parliament in 1919 unanimously asserted its sovereign right to determine that immigrants, regardless of where they came from, might be deported; and parliament declined, the Minister of Justice and many other members of the Liberal party within sound of my voice on the other side declined, to make a distinction for that purpose between immigrants, whether they came from a foreign country or from some other part of the British Empire.
Twenty minutes before the governor general came in.

That happens in all parliaments.

Immigration Act
According to my hon. friend a person bom in Great Britain is subject to deportation though he has been here forty years.
If there is no limitation in the act there should be one.
The old law stated that.

The old law did not in terms; it did only by inference with respect to the alien who becomes naturalized, because the term is five years. It was only three years before, and the definition of citizenship extended the term to five years. I have always been in favour of a limitation with respect to all these matters. There is a limitation in the criminal code, and there should be a limitation of the time within which people may be deported by order in council. I have no doubt as to that; it is one of the matters I was discussing with one of my friends the other day, and if there is no clear limitation in the statute it would be quite right to impose it. However, I desire to press upon the committee the fact that this was an extraordinary enactment to meet extraordinary conditions-which may or may not ever again arise in Canada. When you have a combination of people who wish to destroy government and constituted authority you must have upon the statute books laws which will enable you to meet such a situation. Those who live within the law never need be afraid of it; there have been laws on the statute books of England since 900, continuously in force since the time of Alfred, and laws only apply to those who come within them. Laws are made for the purpose of dealing with those who come within their teTms, and when an extraordinary situation arises-
Mainly one English law which permits a man to be condemned for a criminal offence without trial.
They have the same law providing for deportation from their country that we have in Canada.
Quote it.
I saw men deported from England myself.
British subjects?
I am not talking about British subjects at the moment; I am talking about immigrants. My hon. friend is trying to draw a distinction between two classes of immigrants.
Is a Canadian deportable from England?

I cannot answer that
question; I simply stated that I knew of people being deported from England.
The minister referred to British subjects.

Not until later. Let us have no misapprehension about this. The power of deportation belongs to every sovereign people and is exercised everywhere. Canadians have been sent back from Australia, and last year we sent back to China several people rvho came from Hong Kong. The difficulty is that some of the committee are thinking only of the British Isles instead of British subjects as a whole.
May I ask a question? What distinction does my hon. friend make between a British subject and a Canadian subject?

The distinction is that we are treating all immigrants alike regardless of where they came from. If they came from England they are British immigrants and if they came from the British Empire they are immigrants from the British Empire; they may be white or black, but as far as our power as a parliament is concerned they are on an equality and we have the same right to deport one as the other. Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1910 provided that aliens could be deported without trial, and if it is sound to deport aliens without trial, then those who come into this country and enjoy citizenship because they were born somewhere else should be subject to the same provisions as those who are not naturalized. Otherwise you would encourage one class to preach sedition who could not be dealt with except through trial by jury, while the other class could be deported without trial.
That is what we are doing now.
That is what we are not doing now.
Oh, all right.

It is all right; I am satisfied that hon. gentlemen think it desirable to try to obtain favour from certain classes in the community by saying. "Look at this and that", but the real truth is that this country should treat alike all immigrants who have not become naturalized Canadians or who have not attained the status of Canadians. If we are to deal with the question properly we should define the conditions under which British subjects coming from other parts of the empire may attain the status of Canadians.
Immigration Act
That is what we want.
That is what we want.
I cannot !be a member of this parliament without being a Canadian citizen.

I wonder if the hon.
gentleman realizes that the oath he takes is taken as a British subject?
But how do I vote, if not by virtue of my Canadian citizenship.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I hold in my hand the statutes of 1910, to which my hon. friend has referred. Sections 40 and 41 of chapter 27 of that statute deal with the deportation of prohibited and undesirable classes. In section 40 it was enacted that whenever any person other than a Canadian citizen, within three years after landing in Canada, was convicted of a criminal offence-
Convicted!

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes. It is the following section with which I wish to deal more particularly. Section 41 of the act of 1910 was replaced by the present section 41 which it is now sought to repeal, and it provided that whenever any person other than a Canadian citizen advocated in Canada the overthrow by force or violence of government or constituted authority, and so on, then the complaint must be laid against him and an investigation held, after which he might be deported. I desire to call the attention of the committee first to the words' of section 40:
Whenever any person other than a Canadian citizen-
I would also point to the words of section 41:
Whenever any person other than a Canadian citizen-
Who was a Canadian citizen under the act of 1910? That act provides that a Canadian
citizen is:
(1)	A person born in Canada who has not become an alien;
(2)	A British subject who has Canadian domicile ;
(3)	A person naturalized under the laws of Canada who has not subsequently become an alien or lost Canadian domicile;
So there were three classes of Canadian citizens, first those born in Canada, then those British subjects bom outside of Canada who had acquired Canadian domicile, which at that time was three years and is now five years; and finally, persons naturalized under the laws of Canada. In 1919 this section 41 which it is now sought to repeal was replaced

by a section which enacted that every person who by word or act in Canada sought to overthrow by force or violence government or constituted authority, or who belonged or was suspected of belonging to societies of a certain class, and so on, might be deported. But there was an exception, which provided that the section would not apply to any person who was a British subject either by reason of birth in Canada or by reason of naturalization in Canada. Under the old section 41 no Canadian citizen could be so deported; as my hon. friend said, this applied only to aliens. A Canadian citizen could not be deported and could not be treated as a person desiring to overthrow government by violence and so on unless he was convicted after a fair trial. As I have said, in 1919 this section was replaced, and under that amendment only two classes of Canadian citizens became exempt from that provision, those born in Canada and those aliens who became naturalized in Canada. The second class of Canadian citizens, namely British subjects bom outside of Canada who had acquired Canadian domicile by a residence of five years in Canada, were placed in the same situation as aliens, as men who never had been naturalized and who could be deported by a board of investigation without any trial. That is why this section is so objectionable. I certainly agree with my hon. friend when he says that every country must be mistress of her own citizenship, and must determine who are the people who may become citizens of that particular country I certainly agree with my hon. friend, and that is why we have provisions in our Immigration Act which permit the government of Canada or the Department of Immigration to prevent the entry into Canada of people who are undesirable either by reason of bad health or otherwise. But a man who has been admitted to Canada and has become a Canadian citizen under the law-because the law states that after a domicile of five years he is a Canadian citizen in every respect-must be treated as any other Canadian citizen and must not be deported without being convicted of the offence with which he is charged. Certainly it seems so unfair that one class of Canadian citizen should be considered as inferior to another that merely to set forth the case should be sufficient to convince everybody of the existence of an anomaly. A country cannot be half slave and half free. Surely half of our Canadian citizenship cannot be enjoying certain privileges that are denied to the other half. Canadians are all equal, and that is why we are asking for the repeal of that

Immigration Act
section-in o-rder that those of our citizens who, being British subjects born outside of Canada, have acquired the full right of Canadian citizenship by domicile in this country, should not be made, under this exceptional class, subject to deportation without due form of law.

I am sorry to take up

There has been a good deal of confusion in the discussion because of the different meanings in law of the expression "Canadian citizenship/' "Canadian citizenship'' is used in the Immigration Act in a special sense. It has nothing to do with conferring rights to vote or the right to take part in the nation's business. The Minister of Railways and Canals does not get his right to sit in this house by virtue of the Canadian citizenship which is referred to in the Immigration Act. In the Immigration Act, as the Minister of Justice has explained, "Canadian citizen" means a person born in Canada who has not become an alien, a British subject who has Canadian domicile-which he can get after five years' residence in Canada-or an alien naturalized under the law of Canada. As is well known, in 1918 and 1919 there was a good deal of unrest all over the world. Nearly all of us immediately after the war were looking to reconstruction-that was the word in everybody's mouth-and labour as well as other classes of the community were discussing it. There had been the great turmoil in Russia, and while a good many Canadian workmen did not wish to see the Russian experiment repeated in this country, there is no doubt they were greatly interested in what had taken place over there and frequently discussed it at their meetings. I do not want to enter into the merits of the strike. A strike is a very serious thing, and this strike was a serious thing for Winnipeg. I would say this however: A great many of the citizens, because they did not understand anything about the labour movement, were altogether unfit to judge of the real factors that were at work. When I arrived in Winnipeg it was the third week of the strike and I did not take any very active interest in things until this legislation was passed and the leaders of the strike were summarily arrested, with the idea that they were to be deported. Personally I have never advocated force as a means of bringing about political changes, although others have done so. This government rests upon force; we were told during the war that the only way to overcome our enemies was by means of force. I quoted a passage from a newspaper the other evening in which a gentleman speaking before the St. George's Society in Winnipeg said that force was the only way in which all great reforms had come about in Great Britain, That is common talk, and you cannot wonder that the rank and file of the labour people have followed that teaching and are coming to believe that the only way in which they can gain their ends is by means of force. As I say, I have never taken that view. I do not believe in force to-day as the means of settling international disputes, and I do not believe in force as a means of settling our industrial disputes. I would rather make an appeal to reason, but I know some of our labour people do not hold this view, just as some members of this parliament do not have this view. That is my position, but holding that position I would still say that when there are organizations in this country which are trying to bring about changes to better their conditions, we should surround them with eveiy safeguard in order that they might have the utmost freedom of expression and organization so that they may use what are considered legitimate ways to bring about the desired ends.
In closing, I would say that if you want to create rebellion, then bring in more repressive measures and grind down the people still further. I think none of us wants to do that. Since 1919 industrial commissions have urged time and again that certain changes should be brought about in Canada to better the conditions of the working class, but nothing has been dene along the lines suggested; we are meeting in parliament after parliament, and are doing practically nothing. Is it any wonder that fiery spirits among the

Naturalization Act-Mr. Rinjret
labour people get disgusted with the slow constitutional means, and that occasionally a man gets upon the platform and says something which may 'be construed as being seditious? Let me say that if we are to preserve this country and all that is best in it we must see to it that the common people are given the very fullest opportunities possible. I am very glad that this house has at last come to the point where the majority are willing to remove a piece of legislation which has been a source of irritation and which the labour people feel has been a rank injustice.
