Hon. FERNAND RINFRET (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of Bill No. 19, to amend the Naturalization Act.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition) :
speechtext: Explain.

The object of this bill is
to repeal certain sections of the Naturalization Act whereby applicants for naturalization must appear before the courts of the country and go through a certain procedure before the Secretary of State can finally decide on their applications. This bill has been before the house on several occasions, but has not been very fully discussed, and I think it would be proper, in moving the second reading of the bill, that I should crave the indulgence of the house to bring forward certain facts, documents and arguments which will explain the situation. Perhaps as a preface to my explanation it might be of interest briefly to outline the beginnings of naturalization in this country in so far as the principle of recognition of attained British citizenship is concerned.
Under the French regime, nationality was acquired through individual letters of denization issued by the king. Under the British regime, royal letters patent were also necessary to confer British nationality; and that condition obtained for quite a time. But in Quebec, it seems, according to a letter from Murray, of 1765, that it was sufficient to secure the prerogatives of a British subject, to take the oaths of allegiance and have one's name written in the register kept for the purpose. Evidently this procedure, while conferring certain privileges, did not secure naturalization, which remained a matter reserved to the home government. In the instructions to Lord Dorchester as governor of Lower Canada, 16th September, 1791, clause 17, the king declares "that you do not upon any pretence whatsoever give your assent to any bill or bills that may hereafter be passed by the legislative council and assembly of the province under your government for the naturalization of aliens." This shows that the British government at the time was reserving such bills for the royal assent.

Naturalization Act-Mr. Rinfret
In 1793 an act was passed by the legislature of Lower Canada establishing regulations respecting aliens and obliging them to secure certificates for the time of their residence in Canada. It contained no regulation as to their naturalization. The above act expired in 1795, but was continued to the 7th of May, 1796. It was always necessary to get full naturalization to secure royal letters patent.
I do not think I need go into the matter so extensively as to mention the different acts that were passed in 1817, in 1826, and in 1828, either in Lower or Upper Canada; suffice it to say that during that time all these legislative enactments could not confer anything like naturalization as we understand it to-day, as this was strictly reserved to the British parliament.
In 1844 the British parliament had to deal with the question, a more modern interpretation of the rights and privileges of British subjects being necessary owing to the development of foreign travel, due to the rapid expansion of transportation facilities and the large number seeking British citizenship. Complications apparently arose, and in 1847 the British parliament took cognizance of the colonial measures as being repugnant to the legislation of the home authorities of 1844, especially in regard to the recognition of British citizenship abroad. The principle was definitely and clearly enunciated that any rights of citizenship conferred by the colonies were confined absolutely to the territorial domain of the colony concerned. From this on a certain degree of friction developed as discontent became general over the dual status of naturalized colonials. This dual citizenship did not bother those who remained in the colony, but once a man went abroad he was faced with the situation of being liable for the exactions and laws of his own native country and had no right to the protection of the British flag.
Considerable correspondence was conducted between the colonies and the home authorities, but the British parliament clung to its original position until about 1870, when an act was passed permitting conventions with the various countries arranging for mutual recognition of the right of their citizens to change their allegiance. A minute of council in 1880 reveals a request from the home authorities, suggesting a period of five years residence as a prelude to a treaty between the British parliament and the government of the British dominions. This was agreed to in so far as passports were concerned, the

three year term being retained for civil rights within Canada.
The British authorities, I may explain, went part way in providing a palliative measure by arranging with the consular service to issue passports providing the term of residence abroad did not exceed one year. The principle was thus clearly defined that imperial legislation was supreme even after 1867, when, by the British North America Act Canada was given the right to legislate for the naturalization of aliens. This condition of affairs continued, and it was not until the imperial conference of 1911 that an agreement was reached to establish a citizenship recognizable everywhere. At this conference was urged the recognition of the principle: A British subject anywhere, a British subject everywhere. This view triumphed after a lengthy debate, the British authorities remaining firm in their adherence to the five year term, which was accepted by the dominions. Previously Canada had had a three year term only.
As a prelude to this new understanding, the British parliament passed an act which became the model for the dominions' legislation. The right was reserved at the conference for the dominions to retain full control of local regulations aside from the five years' residence clause, which was made imperative. The British parliament endowed the Secretary of State for Home Affairs with power to grant naturalization, and this method of imposing responsibility on a minister was followed by all the other dominions, with the exception of Canada.
I thought, Mr. Speaker, it would be worth while for me to present these facts in concise form in order that the house may understand the evolution of the granting of naturalization certificates in this country. As I have said, before 1911 naturalization in this country obtained only for local territory and could not in any way confer British citizenship or recognition; and it was only after the conference of 1911 that the British government, in conference with representatives of the different dominions, agreed on certain regulations whereby every dominion would be placed in a position to confer naturalization that would obtain throughout the British Empire. And it was after that conference and in accordance with that principle that in 1914 the then Borden government, through the Hon. Mr. Doherty, presented to this house the bill which became the act under which we are at present working. The essential feature of that bill was, as I have said, to make it possible to confer in this country naturalization that would obtain throughout

Naturalization Act-Mr. Rinjret
the British Empire. Among the qualifications necessary to obtain such naturalization was included the residential clause of five years, which was a new feature in our Canadian legislation. It also contained that very important feature which was new: it granted, after the courts had passed upon the application, discretion to the Secretary of State to refuse naturalization notwithstanding their decision.
The act of 1914 gave to the Secretary of State, under a section which I will read in a moment, absolute discretion to grant or to refuse a certificate of naturalization, but it stipulated that the application could not reach the Secretary of State unless a court of this country had pronounced in favour of it. I contend that when we adopted that dual system in 1914, we were doing something different from what existed in the mother country at that time and from what existed in every other British dominion.
In 1919 certain amendments were proposed; but as they have no bearing on the question which is now before the house, I am merely mentioning the fact. In 1920 the Canadian parliament reverted to the bill of 1914 and we have now in the revised statutes of to-day an act embodying the conditions adopted in 1914 and revived in 1920. If an applicant now desires to obtain naturalization, the procedure is to apply to the department: but before the department of the Secretary of State can pass upon the application it must be submitted to a court, and only when the court has decided whether or not the applicant has the necessary requirements for naturalization can the Secretary of State exercise his discretion. What is proposed by this bill is to do away with the reference to the courts, to do away with the system which has been modelled more or less on the United States system, and to adopt the British system endowing the Secretary of State with full responsibility and discretion as is the case in every other dominion of the empire.
As I have said, this bill has already been before the house several times and I do not think it has yet received proper treatment. It has either been discarded or discussed very rapidly, and I think we owe it to the house and to the principle of the measure to consider it very thoroughly during the course of the present session. By this bill we are seeking to amend our regulations so as to conform to the statutes of the imperial parliament and the other dominions. I do not think it will be necessary for me to indicate the system followed in the other dominions, although I shall do so with pleasure in committee if
hon. members so desire. I have the facts before me but I believe it would only prolong my explanation if I placed them on Hansard now.
What was the system in Canada before 1914?

I have just said that then the * courts were dealing altogether with the matter but they could not confer anything but local citizenship. It was not in their power nor in the power of the government or parliament at that time to confer imperial citizenship in Canada. It was only after the conference of 1911 that the British government and representatives of the different dominions agreed as to certain qualifications that would make it possible for every dominion to confer citizenship and naturalization that would obtain throughout the empire and that would be recognized throughout the world as British citizenship.

Is any time limit
prescribed in this measure? I notice that all the provisions are repealed. Is there any provision for posting applications in the office of the clerk of the court or anywhere else?

Perhaps my hon. friend
will bear with me and I will gradually come to all these matters. 1 am now endeavouring to explain why we are repealing these sections and in due course I will explain what will take place if the house consents to their repeal.

In what way would we
differ from Australia? I can see the great difference between naturalization in England and in Canada. We are a country receiving vast numbers of immigrants whereas in the older countries such a condition does not exist, and we might therefore have to resort to different methods from those employed in the older countries.

It had been my desire
that we should go into committee at once. This would have permitted replies to all these specific questions, but I understand the leader of the opposition because he objects to the principle of the bill or for some other reason, insisted that we should have a discussion on the second reading. Of course my hon. friends will understand that, speaking on the second reading of the bill, I am not in a position to deal with all these points which can be elucidated when we reach the committee stage. But I may tell my hon. friend, as regards the point which he has just raised, that the situation is this. Every dominion retains the control of its local regulations, but

Naturalization Act-Mr. Rinjret
there are certain requirements for British citizenship which are being recognized everywhere. As regards the discretion of the Secretary of State in granting certificates, I have just said that this Dominion is the only one where this is prefaced by a reference to the court. In all the other dominions the Secretary of State has the fullest discretion as to granting certificates. That is the case in Australia, South Africa, and so on.

Is it not true that the
authority still remains with the Secretary of State? All the courts do is to inquire into the fitness of the candidate for citizenship. They hear the evidence in order to find out whether the man is a fit and proper person to receive the citizenship of this country. Having established the proof in that regard, the judge makes a finding and then the Secretary of State still exercises his right to grant or to refuse a certificate. I think that is the practice.

That is the very point
I am going to argue. At present if the court refuses to recommend a certificate, the Secretary of State may not, and according to the interpretation of the act, shall not grant a certificate. He has no discretion when the court refuses to recommend the granting of a certificate.

Does the hon. member
think the Secretary of State, who has not seen nor heard the applicant, should have power to grant the certificate?

If my horn, friend will bear with me, that is the whole purpose of the bill, I will endeavour to explain why that discretion should be given to the Secretary of State. The purpose of these amendments is to make it easier for applicants to obtain naturalization papers. I want to explain what I mean by the word "easier". By that I do not mean for one moment that the requirements will foe any less exacting, or that the qualifications will foe lowered in any way, but we want to establish a procedure whereby every applicant can more easily show to the satisfaction of the Secretary of State and of the government that he possesses the necessary qualifications. It is represented that the present system places difficulties of every kind in the way of applicants. Courts sit at very infrequent intervals, and sometimes at long distances from where the applicants reside, and it makes it very hard for some of them to appear personally before the court, or to be properly represented, which can only be the case under certain circumstances. It

discourages applications for naturalization in a great many instances. I know that every western member -of this parliament, and even some members from the province of Quebec, in parts remote from the big centres, will vouch for what I am saying. That is one of the objections that was raised when this bill was before this house on a previous occasion. I wish to repeat that it is not for one moment intended to make it any easier to obtain a naturalization certificate in the sense that the applicant will not be required to have as firm and strong qualifications, but rather we want to make it easier for every desirable applicant properly to establish his right to a naturalization certificate, which is a very different thing.
We also want to simplify the legal processes; we want to bring about uniformity in administration. At present the requirements for obtaining a certificate, which are to be found in section 4 of the revised statute, are as follows:
The minister may grant a certificate of naturalization to an alien who makes an application for the purpose, and satisfies the minister
(a)	that he has either resided in His Majesty's dominions for a period of not less than five years in the manner required by this section, or been in the service of the crown for not less than five years, within the last eight years before the application; and
(b)	that he is of good character and has an adequate knowledge of either the English or French languages, and,
(cl that he intends if his application is granted either to reside in His Majesty's dominions or to enter or continue in the service of the crown.
I point out at once that certain of these qualifications are of such a nature that they may easily be established, provided that the applicant is acting in good faith. As to whether the applicant has resided for five years within the British Empire, or has resided one year in Canada as required by the act, it is quite immaterial whether that foe established before a tribunal or before the department, but when it comes to paragraph (b), to ascertaining whether he is of good character and has an adequate knowledge of either the English or the French language, that is very much a matter of appreciation, a matter of policy, I should say, rather than a matter of law. I submit that there is nothing in the act to help any judge to decide what is the exact meaning of that provision, "that he is of good character," and is a fit subject for naturalization, and it is therefore very much a matter of policy either for this parliament to pronounce upon, or for this government to take the responsibility for, just as in the same manner it belongs to parliament and to the government to decide whether or not an

Naturalization Act-Mr. Rinjret
alien is a fit subject to be accepted as an immigrant. That is exactly why we desire to repeal these clauses under which it is provided that an applicant must refer his case to the courts. We have had ample proof during the experimental working of this act that there are not, perhaps, two judges in this country who interpret the act in the same way. They have their own opinion as to naturalization; they have their own feeling as to what constitutes a fit subject for naturalization; they have their own appreciation of what constitutes an adequate knowledge of either the English or the French language. So that we have a system under which you may be granted a certificate of naturalization in a certain part of the country, and be met with a very different reception if you apply for it somewhere else. That, I submit is a most undesirable situation.
What steps would the Secretary of State take in order to satisfy himself that the applicant was a fit subject for naturalization? Would he set up a tribune of his own?

That is exactly what I am trying to explain. Rather than leave it to the different judges of the country to give to this act an interpretation which is not uniform, but which is flexible and varies according to the temperament and judgment of the judge, it is desirable that the process of naturalization in this country should issue from one source, that source being the Secretary of State, representing the government of Canada, and responsible to the parliament of Canada. My argument is that the determination of the qualifications for British citizenship in this country is not a matter that should be scattered to the four winds, but rather that it should issue from the one source.
If the house will turn to subsection 3 of section 4, they will find that in 1914 it had been intended to give to the Secretary of State the absolute discretion which we now ask for. Subsection 3, which in my opinion and in the opinion of the department and of a number of legal authorities contains the basic principle of the Naturalization Act as we have it today, reads as follows:
The grant of a certificate of naturalization to any such alien shall be in the absolute discretion of the minister, and he may, with or without assigning any reason, give or withhold the certificate as he thinks most conducive to the public good, and no appeal shall lie from his decision.
Such was the clause which was proposed in 1914, and which was adopted by this house after a considerable discussion. But is it not
evident, and is it not according to what took place in other parts of the empire, that it was the purpose of the bill and the intention of the government of the day, and of parliament which approved the bill, to grant to the Secretary of State the fullest discretion in the matter of naturalization? Look again at the section, which says that it "shall be in the absolute discretion of the minister, and he may, with or without assigning any reason, give or withhold the certificate as he thinks most conducive to the public good, and no appeal shall lie from his decision." That is the clause to which this parliament assented in 1914.
It is true that the same bill did retain the reference to the courts which had existed previously, but if you turn to the explanation of the bill which was given by the Hon. Mr. Doherty, then Minister of Justice, which you will find at page 3250 of volume IV of Hansard of the session of 1914, you will find that he explained it thus:
Perhaps it will be well to point out some of the material differences between the requirements of our existing law and the requirements of this bill. The period of residence differs in term, and differs also with regard to the place in which it must have been passed. The requirement as regards the period of time is that it shall be five years, but that it is sufficient that the last of the five years shall have been passed within the Dominion of Canada. provided the other four years were passed within the British posessions. There are requirements of adequate knowledge of the languages official in the country; in Canada the French and the English languages. The certificates under this legislation are to be issued by the Secretary of State. They are not to emanate directly from the court, but under the sections, which deal with the procedure there, the courts are to be resorted to for the purpose of establishing before them compliance with the essential conditions.
Is it not plain from this explanation that the government was under the impression, and so advised parliament, that the only course the courts could take after the passing of the bill would be to ascertain as to whether there had been essential compliance with those specific requirements, which were mere facts and could be just as well established before the courts as before the department? But as I pointed out a moment ago, that is not what has happened, and the practice of submitting the matter to the courts has not resulted in that unanimity of procedure which should prevail in so important a matter; in short, applicants for naturalization are not treated alike, the practice varying in the different courts. This in my opinion is the main reason why we should amend the act as I have suggested.

Naturalization Act-Mr. Rinjret
I have touched also on the point of simplifying the procedure and making it easier for people to submit their applications for naturalization. Every non. member conversant with conditions obtaining in large sections of the country knows very well that it is difficult, if not almost, impossible, for many applicants either to reach the court or to submit their applications, with the result that undue and undesirable delays occur. In the time at my disposal it would be impossible for me to give in detail the variety of rules obtaining in the courts to which I have just referred, but, as I have said, anyone may go to the department and peruse the files, which reveal the most astounding discrepancies, discrepancies which in some instances confer citizenship cn those not qualified to receive it, and in other cases impose very unfair restrictions on deserving applicants.
One of the most serious grievances in so far as the courts are concerned is that the applicant is compelled to travel long distances, entailing absence from home for one or two days at considerable expense, and quite frequently after going to all this expense and trouble he finds that the court has been postponed or that the naturalization cases have been traversed to the next sitting. This may seem unimportant, but it has the undesirable effect of discouraging applicants to take out naturalization papers. I think it will be generally agreed that when a man has passed the various immigration tests and has fulfilled the requirements of the act as to residence, character and knowledge of one of the official languages, we should make the certificate of naturalization available to him at the least expense and with the least difficulty.
Perhaps I may give a few examples from the extensive file that I have under my hand in order that hon. members may be advised of the discrepancies which I have mentioned. It is represented to the department that many applicants residing at great distances from courts complain of having to go several times to these courts, thus being put to considerable expense. This complaint is very general from all parts of the country, and I have already referred to it. It is also pointed out that owing to the rare visits of the judge in some districts applications have to wait many months before being heard, and on that account applicants are often called to appear at very inopportune times when they are busy at home with the harvest, trapping, or other occupations. Frequently their applications are rejected when they are unable to attend for these reasons, and they are obliged to begin
lMr. Rinfret.]
anew their application at additional expense. This discourages them and some do not proceed further. It is also pointed out that if a judge cannot attend as expected or advertised at the place where application is to be made, applicants are required to travel long distances with their witnesses to meet the judge and have their applications heard at another point rather than wait a year. Through the incompetence of some clerks applications which should not be received are accepted, and finally rejected by the courts or the Secretary of State. Applicants thereby incur expense which would have been avoided had they been properly advised in the first instance. In a number of cases applications are lost and considerable delay results.	[DOT]
As regards the interpretation of the act, I could quote a number of cases, but perhaps it will suffice if I read a memorandum received from the Hon. R. M. Meredith, Chief Justice of the high court division of the supreme court of Ontario, which presents the case in a very convincing way. This document in itself has much intrinsic value, but it has also behind it the very great prestige and authority of a judge who has on very many occasions pronounced himself in regard to naturalization cases, and -who is a perfectly competent authority to speak about the present system. Even if so far my speech had failed to convince the house, I have no doubt this memorandum will do better than I have been able to do myself. Here is what he says:
In the matter of five applications for naturalization under the provisions of the Naturalization Act, 1914.
That which seems to me to be a very unsatisfactory state of the law and practice respecting the naturalization, in Canada, of aliens, impels me to say these things in dealing with and disposing of these applications, which were made at the last Halton autumn assizes;
The act, which is now chapter 138 of the revised statutes of Canada, confers on the Secretary of State the powers and the duty to grant or refuse a certificate of naturalization, upon an application to him-section 4- and after an application to the judge, court, authority or person mentioned in section 22

section 27.
On application to the secretary, naturalization .may be granted on proof of the statutory requirements set but in section 4; namely five years' residence, good character and "an adequate knowledge of either the English or French languages"-the plural number of this word being obviously a clerical mistake for the singular-and intention "to reside in His Majesty's dominions or enter or continue in the service of the crown".
The judges, courts and authorities or persons mentioned in section 22 have now no power to grant naturalization. They have the power and duty to hear and adjudicate upon applications for naturalization conferred on them; but their decision in favour of applicants may in

Naturalization Act-Mr. Rinlret
the "absolute discretion" of the Secretary of State be in effect overruled in a refusal to issue a certificate of naturalization.
Whilst, on the other hand there does not appear to be anything in the way of an overruling in effect by him of a judges or court's decision against an applicant by the simple process of granting another application to him directly under section 4. Nor does there seem to be anything to prevent an applicant, whose application has failed when made to_ a judge or court or authority or person, applying again and again to other judges, courts, authorities or persons; subsection 2 of section 2 of the act does not seem, directly or indirectly, to create a local jurisdiction.
One of the first substantial difficulties met with in the administration of the act is this: judges, courts, etc. must decide "that the alien is a fit and proper person to be naturalized and possesses the proper qualifications" before they can find in favour of applicants: sections 22 and 26: whilst upon an application to the secretary under section 4 all that is required is that the application satisfy him that he has the statutory qualifications which I have before mentioned. But the "absolute discretion'' of the secretary under section 4 subsection 3 gives him the fullest power to refuse any application to him.
So that it is manifest that on every application, such as those I am dealing with, I must find that the applicant not only possesses the required qualification-which I take to mean those set out in section 4-but also is a fit and proper person to be naturalized.
Who is a fit and proper person to be naturalized? Nothing in the act gives any answer to this question. It is not a question of law, nor one of mere eommonsense; it is really a question of policy of the country in which naturalization is sought: and as this Dominion has pqt the matter so completely in the discretion of its secretary of state; sections 4 and 27 of the act, it seemed to me both natural and proper to look to him for knowledge: but so far that looking by me has been in vain. Nor can I find anything that has been said or done by any other judge or any court, authority or person throwing light on the subject, helpful to me. Then unaided in those ways, what am I to decide on the question whether these applicants are "fit and proper persons" to be naturalized under the act, assuming that they possess, as they may, "the required qualifications'' expressed in the act? They are all illiterate, illiterate in the language of their native land, and much more in the language of this province or either of the languages of the Dominion. Nearly all of them work in gangs of men, of their own native language, in brick yards or in other similar employments and generally live in buildings of their employer used in connection with and near to the work in which they are employed; but nothing has been said or discovered against their characters as men in such a condition in life. In early days in this country they would gladly have been naturalized here; as also in the United States of America doubtless, the paramount desire, if not the only one, being, then, to increase the population. But changed times have greatly changed needs and desires in this respect in the United States of America, and here too in a lesser degree, but yet a great change and one much affected too by the experiences and the effect of the most recent great war.
To reach a right conclusion upon this question, it is necessary to bear in mind always the effect of naturalization such as that sought: beside making, as far as this Dominion can, the alien a British subject with all that that means, these things may be mentioned, not all but some of the more important: it gives to the person one of the qualifications to become lawmakers in this Dominion, in the senate, the House of Commons, the provincial legislatures, and the lesser law making councils; a right to vote; a qualification as juror, so that the man may adjudge among his fellow men even in questions of life or death; and a right to fill some public offices; and it prevents expulsion from Canada-deportation, as it is called. It may be said that "deportation" after-five years residence in Canada, or its equivalent, could not be effected; but cases of which I have knowledge show that even fourteen years is not considered a bar by some who exercise the power to deport.
If I acted upon my own views as to what aliens are fit and proper persons to be made British subjects. I should decide against all of the applicants, deeming that the least illiterate of them is not yet qualified.	_
But for two reasons my decision is to be the other way:
1.	Because I have no doubt that a great majority of the hundreds of persons, clothed with the same authority which I am exercising, would so decide in like cases that come before them. As far as T have been able to discover, the general practice seems to be to decide in favour of the applicant when his papers show compliance with the expressed qualifications provided for in the act. And it is of the utmost importance that the law should be administered evenly: that the country should not be open to the reproach: Your laws are uneven.
2.	And because, if the decision were against the applicants, that would probably end the matter, though it should not, for they might make another application, to the secretary direct or to some other judge or court or authority or person having power under the act.
Deciding, as I do, and giving, as I am. my reason for such decision, and making it, in so far as I can, part of that decision, it puts upon the secretary the necessity of either issuing, or refusing to issue, certificates of naturalization, and to that extent disclosing a policy applicable to such applications: and so it may prove to be a step at least towards uniformity in the administration of the law of naturalization in Canada.
This is a long document, Mr. Speaker, but I consider it most interesting and convincing. Chief Justice Meredith, in this statement, is practically recommending himself the very thing we want to achieve by amending the act as we now propose. He has seen the situation very clearly; if the idea which prevailed in 1914 were followed out, it should rest with the court merely to see that the applicant complies with requirements of the law which are facts. As Mr. Justice Meredith puts it, at present the judges also decide as to who is a fit person for naturalization, as to what degree a man seeking naturalization should possess a knowledge of either French,

Naturalization Act-Mr. Rinfret
or English, and as to the character of the applicant. As the learned judge points out, this is not a matter of law; the judge cannot find in the law any enlightenment upon these points; and he cannot receive any help even by applying to the department. He must resort to his own opinions and feelings, and desiring uniformity in the interpretation of the act the judge has decided, without regard to what he thinks about it as an individual, to leave the decisions to the Secretary of State.
That is the decision at which this most learned judge of a very high court in Ontario has arrived. He has not waited for parliament to amend the law as we propose to do; he has done his own amending as to his pronouncements in the granting of naturalization. He has taken the stand that it is not a matter of law so much as a matter of policy, realizing that judges all over the country will decide these points according to their own inclinations. He has declared that so far as he is concerned he is not going to resist any more applications of that kind, in order that they may reach the Secretary of State for decision. I think this is a most important document, and I am quite willing to stand by it in presenting this bill to the house
My hon. friends have put questions as to what will take place if these sections are repealed. I may say that inasmuch as after the court has rendered its decision the Secretary of State still has the discretion to either refuse or grant the certificate, right along we have been conducting our own inquiries in each of the cases presented to the courts. Every one of these cases is now investigated by the department by various methods, either through inquiries made by the mounted police, through arrangements which we have made with homestead inspectors, the records of the immigration department or in other ways at our disposal. This is done in order that we may satisfy ourselves as to the qualifications of the applicants. If this act passed it would simply mean that the applicant would fill out a form, which is quite extensive and covers the whole field of investigation. This form, which is made under oath, is sent to the department, but at present we cannot act upon that application for at least three months, waiting for the decision of the court. If this bill passes the Department of State will be in a position to deal with every case as it comes along and to give every case that degree of attention which it does require in order to make sure of the requirements of the different applicants.
Then there is another feature of the bill, although perhaps this is not quite so 
important: if this amendment carries it will give the state quite an important revenue. At present every applicant must pay $5 before filing his papers, but that is paid to the clerk of the court and only in important centres such as Toronto and Montreal, where the revenues of the clerk exceed $2,000, is any return made to the Department of State. In other cases the amount paid goes to the clerk of the court as a fee for the performance of his work, and this branch of the public service, although it exacts quite a substantial sum of money from such applicants, brings practically no revenue at all to the department. We estimate that if the applications were sent direct, the revenues of the branch probably would cover the cost of the administration and would amount to over $50,000 a year.
I do not know that I should deal with the matter at greater length now. I realize that I have spoken at considerable length. However, I should like to sum up my remarks thus: I claim that the absolute power of granting these certificates should rest with the government through the Secretary of State, and that this is the basic principle of our own act. This is the system followed in Great Britain and in every British dominion. AVhen an immigrant has entered this country according to the regulations of the Department of Immigration and has resided in Canada legally and peacefully for five years, or for one year in Canada and four years in the British Empire, he should be granted a certificate. Uniformity in decision and a greater facility in procedure should be allowed to any such person desiring to become a British citizen. Naturalization is primarily a matter of policy which should rest with the government, and the department would derive an important revenue from the change.
For all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I commend this bill to the attention of the house and feel assured that it will receive the approval of parliament.
Just before the minister closes I should like to ask him a question. Under the new system how long would it take for naturalization papers to go through?
There would be no definite time; that would rest with the department.
It could be done immediately?

Yes. I thank my hon. friend for this question, because in a certain number of cases it has proven a great ineon-

Naturalization Act-Sir George Perley
venience that the department has been unable to grant a certificate to qualified persons simply because of the delay of three months which is provided in the present act, and because of the necessity of referring the matter to the courts.

The minister has made a long explanation of this bill, but I regret to say that he has not brought conviction to my mind. For years this question of naturalization has been a difficult one in this country. Before this last act of 1914, naturalization as granted in Canada carried force in Canada only. Any person naturalized in Canada was no longer a British subject legally when he left this country. That was a condition of affairs that was not satisfactory to anybody, and there was a great deal of agitation about it for a long term of years, as the hon. gentleman will remember. I heard it discussed in this house a good many times. At the imperial conference the matter was brought up from time to time when all the representatives of the dominions were there with those of the mother country, and finally, after a great deal of discussion, they all agreed on a bill of this kind, which if passed by the different dominions and accepted by them would enable the dominions to grant British naturalization which would carry the world over. That was accepted by Canada, and this act of 1914 was passed for that purpose.
To my mind this British naturalization is a very valuable privilege for anybody to have. It carries with it the right to protection all over the world as a British citizen, and it is something that ought not to be lightly given. It is true that the minister ' has the final say in regard to granting these certificates, but he has stated that he wants to follow the practice in Britain. How can anybody compare the situation in Great Britain in this regard with the situation in Canada? Great Britain is a small country, comparatively easy of access in all its parts; distances are not great. Canada is spread over this whole continent from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Somebody in authority must see these applicants individually and personally, in order to determine whether they are fit and proper persons to become naturalized British subjects. It cannot be done by correspondence. It cannot be done by writing to homestead inspectors. It has to be done by someone of real authority, a person who is used to judging character. to judging men; before them these applicants must appear in order that we may be sure that they are fit and proper persons to be naturalized. I quite admit what the 56103-161
minister says about differences of opinion, perhaps, as to exactly what is necessary in order that a person may be regarded as a fit and proper person to be naturalized, but he cannot possibly administer this question in the way that he proposes unless he surrounds himself with a bodyguard of men who can go out into the country and see these applicants; and the men he would have to use for that purpose must be well educated men, men who would command large salaries.
The minister when he was speaking seemed to have it in his mind that perhaps these sections regarding the necessity of going before a judge were not in the act of 1914, and then he said that some of them were. As a matter of fact, if my memory serves me correctly, in the act of 1914 it was provided that the applicant should go to a judge or to a court.

If the hon, member will allow me, I did not intend to give the impression that these clauses were not in the act of 1914. What I tried to express was the fact that these clauses were not fully appreciated, as experience has shown.

Quite so, but they have been in there since we had the power to give complete British naturalization; they were not put in afterwards. In the original act. under which we had the power to naturalize British subjects all over the world, these clauses' appeared and they have been there ever since. I take the point most strongly that every applicant must appear personally before someone in authority, otherwise it is utterly impossible to say whether or not an applicant should be naturalized. I would ask the minister, before whom should an applicant more properly come than before a judge? True, there may be cases in which it is difficult for the man personally to appear before the judge, but section 25 gives the judge discretion. It says that the applicant shall personally appear before the court for examination unless it is established to the satisfaction of the court that he is prevented from so appearing by some good and sufficient cause. In other words, if the judge has evidence from reputable people which satisfies him that this man is for some good reason unable to attend, the judge may go through the evidence and make his report without the man personally appearing. But I feel sure that except in cases' of that kind where the judge thinks it is not necessary, it is absolutely imperative that the applicant should appear personally before someone in authority.
The minister has said that the department carry on investigation themselves. He does

Naturalization Act-Sir George Perley
not mean, I take it, that they do that in all cases. I should be very much astonished to hear that the Department of the Secretary of State did not accept, in almost all cases, the report made by the judge. The judge sees the man personally and talks to him; in the first place he finds out whether the applicant has an adequate knowledge of either the English or the French language. That is of course a basic necessity; no man can become a naturalized British subject unless he has a knowledge of either English or French. That is in the statute, and even if the minister persuades parliament to repeal these other sections, that one will remain. I would ask the minister, is it possible for him to obtain this information by correspondence? The minister says that in some cases he takes the matter up through a member of the mounted police or one of the homestead inspectors. Now, as far as I am concerned, I object most decidedly to an important question of this kind being settled by homestead inspectors. Some of whom would be all right, but many of them are not fitted to decide the questions involved in the granting to these people of British citizenship which is available to them all over the world.
I suppose my hon. friend realizes that the very basis of the application is the affidavit of the applicant himself.
He has to appear in person. We have known cases where a false affidavit has been made.

Then we can revoke the
certificate.

Quite so, but in
that case it is far better that it should never have been granted. If the applicant appears in person before the judge, nothing of that kind will happen. The personal equation cannot be overlooked. We all know a judge can readily decide about a man's character and fitness to become a British subject by meeting him, talking with him face to face and asking him all the questions he desires. The judges all approach this matter with the feeling that they will grant the certificate if at all possible.
I wish they did.

They all approach it with the idea that if the application is in order they will send in a favourable report to the Secretary of State. It is impossible to imagine that any of our judges would deal with any of these applications in any other way, and the minister still retains authority to refuse them.
fSir George Perley.]

mind, not a thousand.

Unfortunately
the Secretary of State is not the man who will make up his mind in regard to it, even if this measure passes. Has he so little to do that he can go and see all these applicants himself? If he does that, we shall not object to the measure; but he is going to allow his mind to be made up for him by somebody else. As I said before he will have to have a large staff and he must have somebody w'ho will go out and interview each one of these men separately. So that when the minister asks me if, as secretary of state, I could make up my mind on the point better than anybody else, I would say to him: Yes, if the man were here and I were talking to him I should be quite willing to deal with. the question myself. But the minister cannot do that; the minister will have placed before him a pile of papers with the name of the applicant, and some of his officials will have recommended the application or said that the certificate should not be granted. How many times will the Secretary of State delve into the whole question himself independently of his officials? I question very much whether he will find time to deal with any of them in that way.
The minister has said that one of the weighty reasons why these sections should be repealed is because applications go astray and that delay is occasioned in consequence. May I ask the minister whether it is not just as

Naturalization Act-Mr. Bennett
likely that an application sent to Ottawa would go astray as an application sent to me of the judges? I cannot see that the Postmaster General would not take the same precautions to have mail delivered to judges as he would to have mail delivered to the Secretary of State. I admit there will he cases wdiero there is delay, with consequent disappointment to the applicant; but that cannot happen very often now, and even if these sections are repealed it will still happen occasionally.
The Prime Minister has asked me about the memorandum from Mr. Justice Meredith. I am not a lawyer, and I am going to leave it to one of the lawyers in the house to comment, on the memorandum and to answer it. It seems to me it is just as much in favour of the present act as it is in favour of the intention of my hon. friend But I will not go into the question myself. There are some things about the present act that I like very much. In the first place section 23 reads:
The application shall be delivered at the office of the clerk or other proper officer of the court during office hours, and such application shall be posted by such clerk or other proper officer in a conspicuous place in his office, continuously for a period of at least three months before the application is heard by the court.
The delay is very necessary in order that everybody may know that the man has made an application for naturalization. I remember a case where people objected to a man being naturalized, and unless a notice was posted up and an opportunity given to people interested to object, how is it possible to put into effect section 24, which reads:
At any time after the filing of any such application and previous to the hearing of the application, any person objecting to the naturalization of the alien may file in court an opposition in which shall be stated the grounds of his objection.
Does the minister think that is not a salutary clause? Surely the neighbours, the people who know the man well, are able to judge whether he should properly be naturalized or not, and if there is any feeling amongst the people in the community who know him that he should not be naturalized, an opportunity should be given to them to appear before the judge and to state their reasons.
The minister says that if these sections are repealed the department will make a good deal of revenue. I fancy that the clerks of the courts need the revenue they get for this service more than my hon. friend's department, Moreover. I take issue with him as to the revenue being sufficient to provide the expenses of administration; if his proposed bill becomes law. I predict that he will have to 56103-1611
insert in the estimates an item to carry on this work. That is to say-and I come back to what I started with-he will have to increase his staff; there will have to be provision in the estimates for more assistance and more expenses for people going about this country to interview these men, unless he intends to act on the correspondence he receives and not to have anybody interview them personally. If he does not have them interviewed personally he will make many mistakes and many people will be naturalized in this country who ought not to be.
I feel strongly that British naturalization, good throughout the world, is a most valuable privilege and should be hedged around with all reasonable precautions to ensure that certificates are not granted to undesirable people. The minister says: Oh, we have the power to revoke them. I know that, and occasionally one has to be revoked, but to revoke a certificate is a very serious step to take. It is far better that the investigation be made beforehand so that certificates will not be granted to people who will make undesirable citizens. Therefore I urge the minister to reconsider the matter. So far as I know the present act, on the whole, has worked well. There may have been a few cases where some hardship has resulted, but it is a great deal better to have delayed the naturalization papers of a few who perhaps are not entitled to naturalization than to have a, lot of people naturalized who ought never to be naturalized.

It certainly was my intention to speak on the second reading of this measure. The objection to it. is an objection in principle, and, particularly in view of the fact that the bill contains only one section, it should have been far better to divide the house on the second reading. It is true that the opportunity will be afforded to us on the third reading; we can move the six months' hoist 'then as readily as we could have moved an amendment on the second reading. There was no such urgent necessity as seemed to be apparent of declaring the second reading carried, when some of us had made up our minds to speak on the motion for the second reading; however, that is not a matter of very great importance.
Naturalization with some people in Canada has been treated as a joke. I can recall my early days in western Canada, before the
2542	COMMONS
Naturalization Act-Mr. Bennett
statute was amended, when it was only necessary to made a declaration before a justice of the peace or a commissioner for taking affidavits, and a long line of people would gather before the court. Sometimes only the certificate would be read, and then naturalization would be granted upon the payment of a fee of $2. Under these conditions naturalization became a sort of by-word and reproach. Men were gotten together in a political hall on a given night, they took the declaration and signed the papers; the papers were put before a judge, and times without number it has been discovered that the affidavits were false and the declarations wholly erroneous.
In 1914, following the imperial conference of 1911, the British parliament passed a statute with respect to naturalization. It was a matter that had engaged the attention of Sir Wilfrid Laurier for many years, and if those who are anxious to pursue the history of the subject will read what was said by Sir Wilfrid Laurier on many occasions, they will ascertain why. Up until 1914, when this parliament passed the present Naturalization AcL it was possible to confer Canadian citizenship only upon those who were naturalized. That Canadian citizenship ceased when the person to whom it was granted passed beyond the three mile limit and was no longer within the territorial jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada. It was that objection, of course, that was urged by the Americans who came to settle here. It was said that they had lost their own citizenship; they passed out of the three mile limit, and then the question was, what citizenship did they possess? It was contended by some that their American citizenship was renewed.
Then you had the immigrant that came to us from Europe. He came from communities where they had compulsory military service, and I recall many of the difficulties that arose, after the war broke out, in connection with that particular matter. Under the laws of some of the kingdoms of Europe it is provided that notwithstanding the fact that its nationals may obtain naturalization under such conditions as it was granted in this country prior to 1914, they still were within the reach of the army of the country whence they came. The result was that some who went from this country the possessors of Canadian naturalization certificates found themselves, as soon as they arrived in the land whence they originally came, subject to compulsory military service and compelled to undergo training as required by the law of that country.	_
This matter, of course, engaged the attention of our statesmen for a. number of years. It was the subject of much discussion at many

imperial conferences, and finally in 1911 it was decided at the conference that the subject matter should be dealt with in a manner that would permit any person who was naturalized in any one of the king's dominions to obtain thereby naturalization throughout the British Empire; in other words, he became a British subject throughout the world. He was no longer a Canadian citizen. He obtained all the rights, all the privileges, all the claims, if he were naturalized in Canada, as though he were born within the sound of Bow Bells. There was no distinction between the two. That was a very, very great advance. It carried with it enormous obligations on the part of the British government; for while we were obtaining all the benefits, we were at the time providing no machinery for the protection of the citizen. Our flag did not carry protection upon the high seas. Nothing of that sort, so far as we were concerned, was being put forward. It therefore became essential that an agreement be arrived at whereby the mother statute-if I might use a term which, while not very elegant, adequately expresses the meaning-should be passed by the British parliament, and that the parliaments of the self-governing dominions would pass a statute practically similar in terms, so far as essentials were concerned, but varying in the regulations by which naturaliazation was made effective. The parliament of Great Britain therefore passed in 1914 the statute which I have under my hand.
